extraction.name: PIQA: Physical Interaction Question Answering
extraction.description: PIQA is a benchmark dataset for evaluating physical commonsense reasoning in natural language understanding systems. It consists of multiple-choice questions where a model must choose the most appropriate solution to a physical goal from two options. The dataset is inspired by instructables.com and uses adversarial filtering (AFLite) to remove annotation artifacts.
extraction.creator: Yonatan Bisk, Rowan Zellers, Ronan Le Bras, Jianfeng Gao, Yejin Choi (Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Microsoft Research AI, Carnegie Mellon University, University of Washington)
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Annotators were provided prompts derived from instructables.com and asked to construct goal-solution pairs. They wrote a physical goal, a valid solution, and an invalid 'trick' solution that sounds plausible but is physically incorrect. Data was collected in batches and validated by other annotators. AFLite was applied to remove annotation artifacts.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Instructions from instructables.com were used as prompts/seeds for human annotators to construct goal-solution pairs.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: AFLite algorithm was applied to remove annotation artifacts and spurious biases. It discards instances whose feature representations are collectively highly indicative of the target label, using an ensemble of linear classifiers trained on BERT-Large embeddings.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Examples with low agreement during validation were removed. AFLite was applied using 5,000 examples to fine-tune BERT-Large and compute embeddings of remaining instances to remove biased examples. Train, development, and test folds were automatically produced by AFLite.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were shown an instructable for inspiration and asked to provide: (1) a physical goal, (2) a valid solution, and (3) a 'trick' — an invalid solution that sounds plausible but is physically wrong. Annotators were seeded with instructables from six categories (costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop). A qualification HIT was required before participation. Data was validated by other annotators for correctness.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Examples with low agreement during validation were removed. Users with low agreement were de-qualified. Human performance was calculated by majority vote among annotators who achieved 90% on the qualification HIT.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Spacy (tokenization), GPT BPE tokenizer, BERT-Large (for AFLite embedding computation)
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Reporting bias was identified as a major issue: when thinking about how to achieve a goal, people are drawn to prototypical solutions and common tools, rarely considering the full range of everyday objects. AFLite was applied to reduce annotation artifacts and stylistic biases.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset focuses on English only. Some correct examples requiring expert-level domain knowledge were removed during validation as they fall outside 'commonsense.' The dataset was constructed to be adversarial to BERT. Future models may surpass human performance by finding large in-domain data sources.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for benchmarking and evaluating physical commonsense reasoning in natural language understanding models. It can be used for training, validation, and testing of NLP models. It also serves as a diagnostic tool for probing physical knowledge in pretrained language models.

name.evidence: We introduce the task of physical commonsense reasoning and a corresponding benchmark dataset Physical Interaction: Question Answering or PIQA.

description.evidence: We introduce a new dataset, PIQA, for benchmarking progress in physical commonsense understanding. The underlying task is multiple choice question answering: given a question q and two possible solutions s1, s2, a model or a human must choose the most appropriate solution, of which exactly one is correct.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: We asked annotators to provide semantic perturbations or alternative approaches which are otherwise syntactically and topically similar to ensure physical knowledge is targeted. The dataset is further cleaned of basic artifacts using the AFLite algorithm.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: Our dataset is inspired by instructables.com, which provides users with instructions on how to build, craft, bake, or manipulate objects using everyday materials. We asked annotators to provide semantic perturbations or alternative approaches.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: Our goal is to construct a resource that requires concrete physical reasoning. To achieve this, we provide a prompt to the annotators derived from instructables.com. The instructables website is a crowdsourced collection of instructions for doing everything from cooking to car repair.

rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: The dataset is further cleaned of basic artifacts using the AFLite algorithm introduced in (Sakaguchi et al. 2020; Sap et al. 2019)... AFLite uses an ensemble of linear classifiers trained on random subsets of the data to determine whether these pre-computed embeddings are strong indicators of the correct answer option.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed from the data... we use 5,000 examples from the original dataset to fine-tune BERT-Large for this task and compute the corresponding embeddings of all remaining instances... the train, development, and test folds were automatically produced by AFLite.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: annotators are asked for 1. a physical goal, 2. a valid solution, and 3. a trick. The trick should sound reasonable, but be wrong often due to a subtle misunderstanding of preconditions or physics. Additional HITs (not shown) were run for qualification prior to this stage and validation afterwards.

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: Annotator pay averaged >15$/hr according to both self-reporting on turkerview.com and our timing calculations.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed from the data... Human performance was calculated by a majority vote. Annotators were chosen to participate that achieved 90% on the qualification HIT from before.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: Our goals, as tokenized by Spacy, average 7.8 words... Figure 4 shows a plot of the correct and incorrect sequence lengths (as tokenized by the GPT BPE tokenizer)... we use 5,000 examples from the original dataset to fine-tune BERT-Large for this task and compute the corresponding embeddings of all remaining instances.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: we initially experimented with asking annotators for (task, tool) pairs via unconstrained prompts, but found that reporting bias swamped the dataset... We use AFLite to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples from the data, which have been shown to artificially inflate model performance on previous NLI benchmarks.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: all data was collected in English... During validation, examples with low agreement were removed from the data. This often meant that correct examples were removed that required expert level knowledge of a domain (e.g. special woodworking terminology) which should not fall under the umbrella of 'commonsense.'

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: We introduce a new dataset, PIQA, for benchmarking progress in physical commonsense understanding... The setup of PIQA allows us to use it to probe the inner workings of deep pretrained language models, and to determine the extent of their physical knowledge... In total our dataset is comprised of over 16,000 training QA pairs with an additional 2K and 3k held out for development and testing, respectively.
